data.title: A small press with a wide window.
data.intro: Cord & Page is a fictional independent publisher of fiction, nonfiction and poetry, used here to show how the theme looks with content.

children.text: We publish a few books each year, chosen because we cannot stop thinking about them. Our list is small on purpose: every title is read twice, edited carefully and printed on paper that feels like the book.
What we publish

Novels, narrative nonfiction, essays and poetry from writers whose voices are not yet widely heard. We are drawn to books that look closely at ordinary life and find it more interesting than expected.
How we work
We work with authors from the first draft to the last proof, and with independent bookshops and libraries long after publication.
Submissions

We read unsolicited submissions twice a year. Send a short note about your book, a sample chapter of up to 5,000 words and a line about yourself. Use the contact page and choose Submissions, and your message will reach the editors directly.
We cannot reply to every submission in detail, but we read each one. Sample details on this page are fictional.

data.title: Usage and credits
data.intro: How the sample content in this theme should be read.

children.text: Cord & Page, its authors, books, journal posts and contact details are fictional and exist only to demonstrate the theme. Phone numbers use a fictional 555 range and email addresses use the .example domain.
Book cover art and photographs are AI-generated illustrations prepared for the ZeroHostCMS preview collection. Replace them with your own cover images and photographs before publishing.
Fonts
Newsreader and Inter are used under the SIL Open Font License 1.1 and served from the site itself.

data.title: The River Between
data.author: l-k-hart
data.summary: Two sisters, one valley and the river that decides what each of them keeps.
data.synopsis:
When their father's farm is sold, Mara and Ines return to the valley where they grew up. The river that divides the land has been rising for years, and so has the silence between them.

Over one long summer, the sisters walk the old boundaries, open the locked rooms of the house and discover what each has been carrying alone. A quiet, absorbing novel about family, inheritance and the places that hold us.

data.title: A Brighter Silence
data.author: n-sato
data.summary: Poems about listening, late light and the quiet after long conversations.
data.synopsis:
A Brighter Silence gathers sixty short poems written over six winters. They begin with a kettle, a window and a letter left unanswered, and widen toward the people we keep company with.

Spare, warm and precise, these poems ask what it means to listen well, and what is left when the talking stops.

data.title: The Long Way Home
data.author: d-ellis
data.summary: A walking memoir along a coastline that keeps changing shape.
data.synopsis:
D. Ellis sets out to walk the same stretch of coast every week for a year. The cliffs fall, the tide tables shift and the walker slowly learns what home might mean.

Part memoir, part field guide, The Long Way Home is a book about attention: to weather, to neighbours, and to the slow work of belonging somewhere.

data.title: Small Kindnesses
data.author: e-marlowe
data.summary: Twelve essays on the everyday gestures that hold a neighbourhood together.
data.synopsis:
A borrowed ladder, a note on a windscreen, a pot of soup left on a doorstep. E. Marlowe writes about the small acts that rarely make the news and quietly shape our days.

Funny, observant and generous, these essays make a case for paying attention to the ordinary.
data.subtitle: Essays for a brighter ordinary

data.title: The Quieter World
data.author: n-sato
data.summary: Night, sea and the hush between waves: poems for a quieter world.
data.synopsis:
Written at the edge of a dark sea, The Quieter World follows a single night from dusk to first light. The poems are short, steady and full of weather.

A companion to A Brighter Silence, and a collection to read slowly, ideally late.
data.subtitle: Poems

data.title: Maps of Belonging
data.author: t-adeyemi
data.summary: A novel in three journeys about the maps we draw to find our way home.
data.synopsis:
Three people, three journeys and one hand-drawn map passed from stranger to stranger. As the map is copied, corrected and argued over, each traveller redraws their idea of home.

An inventive, tender novel about migration, memory and belonging.
data.subtitle: A novel

data.title: Field Notes for Neighbours
data.author: a-brandt
data.summary: Observations and small experiments for living well with the people next door.
data.synopsis:
What happens if you knock on the door beside yours? A. Brandt spent a year finding out, keeping notes on shared gardens, street parties and the etiquette of the borrowed ladder.

A short, practical and warm book for anyone who wants their street to feel more like a neighbourhood.

data.title: L. K. Hart
data.intro: Writes novels about families, landscapes and the things that travel between them.

children.text: L. K. Hart writes fiction set in river valleys and small towns, where a place shapes the people who stay and the people who leave. The River Between is the first novel to be published by Cord & Page.
Hart lives in a farmhouse at the end of a long lane and writes in the early mornings, before the post arrives.

data.title: N. Sato
data.intro: Poet of light, listening and the quiet that follows a long conversation.

children.text: N. Sato is a poet whose short, patient poems are built from small observations: a window at dusk, a neighbour's laughter through a wall, the pause before someone answers.
Sato has two collections with Cord & Page, A Brighter Silence and The Quieter World, and teaches evening poetry workshops at a community library.

data.title: D. Ellis
data.intro: Walks coastlines and writes about what changes and what stays.

children.text: D. Ellis writes narrative nonfiction about walking, weather and the slow work of coming home. The Long Way Home follows a year of walking the same stretch of coast.
Ellis keeps a paper notebook for every walk and says most of the book was written standing up.

data.title: E. Marlowe
data.intro: Essayist of ordinary days, small gestures and the people who make them.

children.text: E. Marlowe writes essays about everyday kindness, from the neighbour who waters your plants to the stranger who holds a door. Small Kindnesses collects twelve of them.
Marlowe works part-time at a village bookshop and writes on the bus.

data.title: T. Adeyemi
data.intro: Novelist of maps, migration and the many meanings of home.

children.text: T. Adeyemi writes novels about people who live between places and the maps they draw to find their way back. Maps of Belonging is a novel in three journeys.
Adeyemi grew up speaking three languages and writes in whichever one the scene demands.

data.title: A. Brandt
data.intro: Writes practical, warm nonfiction about living well with the people next door.

children.text: A. Brandt writes nonfiction about neighbourhoods: the shared garden, the street party, the borrowed ladder. Field Notes for Neighbours is a short book of observations and small experiments.
Brandt organises a monthly street swap and is rarely without a clipboard.

data.title: Why we publish slowly
data.summary: A few books a year, read twice and edited once more than we think we need to.

children.text: We publish a handful of books a year. People sometimes ask whether that is a limit or a choice. It is a choice, and this note explains why.
Reading twice

Every manuscript is read at least twice by different editors, a few weeks apart. The first read tells us whether we are moved. The second tells us whether we are still moved once the novelty has worn off.
Editing once more
We almost always edit one more time than the schedule asks for. The last pass is usually the smallest, and it is usually the one an author thanks us for.
None of this is fast. We think readers can tell.

data.title: Notes from the proof desk
data.summary: What happens between the final manuscript and the first printed copy.

children.text: The proof desk is a small table by the window with a pencil, a ruler and a vase that is never empty. It is where a manuscript becomes a book.
Reading aloud
Proofs are read aloud, line by line, by one person while another follows on the page. It is slow and a little theatrical, and it catches things that silent reading misses.
The last comma
There is always a last comma. We have learned to leave it for the morning.

data.title: A reading list for the quieter months
data.summary: Seven books for long evenings, from poetry to walking memoirs.

children.text: As the evenings draw in, we reach for books that reward patience. This is the list on the editors' table this month.
To read slowly
Poetry, mostly: small books that fit in a coat pocket and repay a second reading.
To read in one sitting
A novel set along a river, a walking memoir and a book of essays about neighbours.
Some are ours. Most are not. Ask at your local bookshop and they will know what to put in your hands.

data.title: Choosing paper that feels like the book
data.summary: Why a book of poems and a novel should not be printed on the same stock.

children.text: Paper is the first thing a reader touches and the last thing they think about. We think about it a great deal.
Warm, not bright
We favour warm, uncoated stock that takes ink softly and does not glare under a lamp.
Weight matters
A book of poems should feel light enough to carry everywhere. A novel can be a little more generous.
Small decisions, repeated, are most of what a book is.

data.title: How a title finds its cover
data.summary: Covers begin as conversations, not briefs, and sometimes as a walk.

children.text: The cover of a book is a promise. We try to keep it quietly.
Start with a conversation
We ask authors what the book looks like in their head. The answers are often a place or a colour rather than an image.
Then a walk
For one of our nonfiction titles, the editor and the designer walked the coastline in the book before sketching anything.
The best covers feel as though they were always going to be that way.
